newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - April PPI to show milder price pressures.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - April PPI to show milder price pressures.

text.p: Another month of scant inflationary pressures at the wholesale level is expected for April, as factors seen in March look to have disappeared, analysts said.

Producer prices are expected to have fallen 0.1 percent in April, with the PPI excluding food and energy seen up 0.1 percent. Intermediate and crude prices also look to be well behaved, analysts said.
In March, the overall PPI fell 0.1 percent but the "core" rate was up 0.4 percent.
The PPI data are due Wednesday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT and are sandwiched between reports on retail sales and consumer prices on Tuesday and Thursday, respectively.

"There are no visible signs of an acceleration in inflation," said Ram Bhavagatula, chief financial economist at Citicorp. Over the past 12 months, PPI finished good inflation has risen just 1.5 percent.

Analysts cited a fall in energy prices -- seen down more than 1 percent -- as the main factor behind the expected fall. Plus, they predicted, with spot commodities prices mostly lower in April, food prices should also post a decline.
Meanwhile, special one-time factors such as civilian aircraft and tobacco prices, which rose in March, thereby pushing up the core index, are not expected to be a factor in the upcoming report.
"Judging from the prices paid component in NAPM, there are very little pressures in the pipeline," said Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Nesbitt Burns Securities.
Brian Fabbri, chief economist at Paribas, said that consumer goods prices should show some modest increases, mostly due to the usual summer apparel price hikes.
Still, some see a risk to the subdued inflation picture.

Noralyn Marshall, an analyst at Scotia Capital Markets, in noting the large price increases in tobacco and aircraft in March, "with higher levels of capacity use and strong growth in profits and incomes, we may see more impact from what appears to be 'one-off' price hikes, as firms test the market for price increases that will stick."
Bond prices are said to reflect a string of weak reports this week.

"Any positive number (on PPI) will be pretty disappointing," said John Williams, chief global economist at Bankers Trust Co. "With the FOMC meeting coming up next week, it wouldn't take much to spook people."
